idiom_name: one type parameter (or one type) per state + private constructors + consuming transitions
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each state its own marker type or class, carry the current state as a type parameter of the protocol value (or as the concrete class of the value), and expose each legal transition only on the source state so the destination state's type is the return type. Transitions must consume or re-emit the value - if the old state stays usable, the guarantee is gone. Keep constructors private or behind a factory so the only way in is the initial state, and fall back to an enum plus exhaustive branching for transitions that depend on runtime data.
code_sketch:
struct Handle<State> { ... }                 # state is part of the type
open(h: Handle<Closed>) -> Handle<Open>      # exists only for Closed
lock(h: Handle<Closed>) -> Handle<Locked>    # exists only for Closed
# constructor is private: callers cannot create Handle<Open> directly
pitfalls: Transitions that keep the same type must still consume or return the value; leaving the source usable silently drops the guarantee.
A public constructor or public marker lets callers enter any state directly.
Runtime-decided transitions cannot be encoded as types - branch on an enum instead of forcing a type-level state.

Wrong move: encoding a runtime-decided transition as typestate anyway and casting, downcasting or using unsafe to reach the state you need -> the code compiles but the guarantee is erased at exactly the branch every later consumer depends on -> instead model the runtime decision as an enum with explicit branching and keep typestate only for the statically visible sequence.

Wrong move: keeping distinct typestate types once values must live in one collection or one loop variable -> states share no supertype so the code will not compile, and the tempting fix is a boxed common interface that erases the state -> instead erase to a runtime representation (enum or erased handle with guards) precisely at the collection boundary.
